title: Crumb coating a layer cake
subtitle: the thin first coat that locks in loose crumbs
excerpt: A crumb coat is a thin layer of buttercream or ganache spread over a freshly filled layer cake to seal in any loose crumbs before the final decorative coat goes on. It takes ten minutes and makes the finished surface smooth and crumb-free. The cake goes into the fridge for twenty minutes between the two coats.
sourceNotes: Standard layer-cake technique found in British and American cake-decorating manuals from the 1960s onward. The two-coat method is the professional bakery standard.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin first layer of buttercream or ganache applied to a filled layer cake to trap loose crumbs before the final decorative coat.
The process of stacking cake sponges with filling between each layer and levelling them before coating.

content.text: is a thin, rough first layer of buttercream spread over a stacked cake to seal any loose crumbs against the sponge. The cake then chills until the coat firms up, so that the final smooth coat goes on clean with no crumbs dragging through it.
The coat does not need to look neat. It is the most forgiving step in
: its only job is containment. Aim for about 3 mm thick all over: enough to seal crumbs, thin enough to set quickly in the fridge.
Stack your sponge layers with filling between each one and level the top by pressing gently with your hand or a board. The cake should sit flat on a cake board.
Place the board on a turntable if you have one. If not, work on a clean board raised on an upturned bowl so you can reach all sides without tilting the cake.
Place a large spoonful of buttercream on top of the cake. Spread it out to the edges with a palette knife, then push it down over the sides in downward strokes.

Work around the sides, adding small amounts of buttercream and spreading them thin. Do not try to fill gaps or get a smooth finish yet. A scraper drawn lightly around the sides will even out obvious bumps.
The coat is done when the entire surface of the cake is covered, even if crumbs show through. Do not go back over areas repeatedly, as this drags crumbs into the buttercream.
Put the cake in the fridge, uncovered, for 20 to 30 minutes, until the crumb coat is firm and dry to the touch. In a cool kitchen you can chill for 15 minutes; in a warm kitchen allow 30.
Apply the final coat as usual: load fresh buttercream onto the top, smooth it down the sides, and finish with a scraper drawn steadily around once. The crumb coat beneath holds everything stable.

attrs.problem: Crumbs still appearing in the final coat
attrs.avoid: Avoid rushing the chill time; if the crumb coat is not firm, it will not contain crumbs.
attrs.fix: Return the cake to the fridge for a further 15 minutes before applying more buttercream.

attrs.avoid: Avoid cold buttercream straight from the fridge; it will drag and tear.
attrs.fix: Beat the buttercream briefly at room temperature until it is soft and spreadable before applying.

attrs.avoid: Avoid building a tall cake with no support; layers need to be level before stacking.
attrs.fix: Place a small dot of buttercream on the board before setting the bottom layer on it.
